idea: Japan's "negative spread". Life insurers promised about 4% (5.5-6.5% pricing in 1995) on money still to be invested, while assets earned about 2% after 1990. The gap hit the whole book for a decade. Nissan Mutual failed on 25 April 1997, the first postwar life-insurer failure, and others followed.
sources: Nippon Life Research Institute report id=51079; Nogami, SOA International Section News, May 2016; Wikipedia "Nissan Life"; CEPII letter 196 (2000)
use: The coupon soft spot at full scale. Japan's gap was on 100% of the book every year; Laura's is on the reinvested coupons only, once (TNA note 1 names this risk). Laura's own size: a 2pt fall in yields costs about $21k of the $500k (IPS_number_sheet, 16 Oct; MODEL, old design). Device: a table of a 1989 insurer beside Laura, same promise length, same 2pt fall.
critique: It was not only rates: property, loan and share losses, and policy surrenders, all played a part. CEPII's "Ponzi-style" is a journalist's word. Counts differ (8 failures per Nogami; "six of the eighteen" per CEPII). Chiyoda failed probably in October 2000, not 1999. Window: Nogami says JGBs rose from 11% to 42% of life insurers' asset mix 1995-2015, which is not "the survivors then bought".
verified: VERIFIED (S1 opened NLI, the SOA pdf, Wikipedia and CEPII); counts CONFLICTING

idea: Dutch funding-ratio zones and conditional indexation. A fund's one number is assets over liabilities (x100%). Below about 104% the fund must take measures; between 104% and 110% there is no indexation; at 110% or more, indexation may be granted. The Dutch abandoned the regime: under the new system "the funding ratio no longer determines whether benefits rise or fall".
sources: De Nederlandsche Bank, "pensions funding ratio" page (paraphrase); Future of Pensions Act detail UNVERIFIED (Houthoff page not opened)
use: The cliff lesson: share a fixed fraction (half the shares) rather than all or nothing at a line. A three-zone "repair / hold / share" picture for co-sponsors.
critique: The thresholds are cliffs. The ratio moved with the discount rate, so cuts came when yields fell. Indexation means inflation-linking, which Laura's nominal payments lack. The procyclicality story comes from background reading and was not re-verified.
clash: Partly. A "repair" zone implies trading in response to a ratio, and the FINAL allows only two reasons to change. Use only the "half, not all" sharing lesson.

idea: Germany's maximum guaranteed rate (Höchstrechnungszins). The regulator caps what an insurer may guarantee at a cautious portfolio's expected yield less a 40% safety margin (at least 0.4pt in low-rate phases). The rate was 4.00% from July 1994 to June 2000, 3.25% from July 2000, 2.25% in 2007-11, 0.90% in 2017-21, 0.25% in 2022-24 and 1.00% in 2025; the DAV recommends 1.0% for 2027.
sources: DAV (German Actuarial Association), "Höchstrechnungszins in der Lebensversicherung" pdf; PwC Germany insurance-news blogs (articles 240720 and 252092)
use: Answers "why promise only half?". Regulators haircut what may be promised because sellers under competitive pressure cannot be trusted to cap themselves. The top of Laura's band is her own maximum guaranteed rate, and the FINAL's kept half is her haircut: the same instinct, not the same number.
critique: It protects new customers only, and it is blunt (one rate for all). It fell to 0.25%, making guarantees almost unsellable. The 40% is a judgement. The Swiss BVG comparison was not opened.
verified: VERIFIED (S1; paraphrase of the DAV and PwC pages)

idea: Ruin theory with risky investment. With the reserve in cash, the chance of ruin falls exponentially as capital grows; with the reserve in a risky asset it falls only as a power, and if 2a/sigma^2 < 1, ruin is certain.
sources: Frolova, Kabanov and Pergamenshchikov, "In the insurance business risky investments are dangerous", Finance and Stochastics 6 (2002) 227-235; arXiv 2012.05083 (intro); arXiv 1505.04331
use: "Cushion in bonds, shared upside in shares", and "you cannot buy certainty in the asset that is trying to beat you" (a short Portfolio Analysis box).
critique: The result is asymptotic and assumes an infinite horizon, random claims and premium income, none of which Laura has. Window 28 Oct: an analogy, not a theorem-backed reason. The 1-in-10 to 1-in-100 figures are illustrations only.
verified: VERIFIED (S1 opened the DOI abstract and the arXiv intros)

idea: Solvency II's two boxes. A cash flow that "can be replicated reliably" using instruments with an observable market value is valued at the copy's price, with no separate risk margin. Only what cannot be copied (policy options, mortality, expenses) carries a margin.
sources: Directive 2009/138/EC Art. 77(4) (legislation.gov.uk); Delegated Regulation 2015/35 Art. 40 (paraphrase)
use: Ten fixed nominal $50k payments are the cleanest replicable cash flow there is, and Treasuries are the copy, so the price of the promise is the price of the ladder. Coupon reinvestment is the part not replicated "in amount and timing", and its reserve is Laura's "risk margin" (the $10k-$20k hold-back option, number sheet decision 3; MODEL, old design). Device: a two-column page, "bought" and "reserved".
critique: Art. 40 says nothing about coupon reinvestment. "Replicable" is a judgement. The risk margin's calibration is a policy number.
verified: VERIFIED (77(4) quoted from legislation.gov.uk; Art. 40 paraphrased)
clash: No: the bought box is the FINAL's LADDER and FLOOR. Any hold-back sizing is not in the FINAL.
note: VOID figure (NUMBERS.md 9 Nov): $10k-$20k hold-back is now Keel's margin of $21,149 (section 2)

idea: The zero-premium stress test. Solvency II Art. 18 does not count a future premium the payer cannot be compelled to pay, so count the 2028 deposit as zero and ask "would the payments hold if it never arrived?"
sources: Delegated Regulation 2015/35 Art. 18 (legislation.gov.uk); R06 and L-10 (22 Oct curve)
use: Honest answer for the FR: usually, not always. The ladder costs more than $300k in 46-47% of paths (median gap about $9.8k), filled from the 2028 deposit. A cheque breaks only if yields fall about 2pt and the deposit falls by more than about 56% (M3); with a coverage rule the cheques survive a deposit of about $40k (M5). All MODEL, old design. This ties CAREER to COMPLETE2028, since the 2028 deposit is career income.
critique: Window 28 Oct: S1's "Yes" is FALSE on Keel's own numbers. Art. 18 is an analogy, not an authority.
verified: Art. 18 VERIFIED; S1's answer CONFLICTING (corrected by the Window and FUSIONS Conflict 1)
clash: YES as S1 wrote it ("the ladder is bought from the 2027 money alone"): the FINAL says the 2028 deposit completes the ladder if yields fall. The corrected form fits.
note: VOID figure (NUMBERS.md 9 Nov): ladder over $300k in 46-47%; break if the deposit falls over 56% after -2pt is now $2,287 over now and a 53% threshold (sections 1 and 5)

idea: Deferred income annuities and mortality credits: seems relevant (a lump sum now, fixed income later), isn't. Without a mortality pool, an annuity is a ladder plus the insurer's margin, and annuities are not WInS-permitted.
sources: Kitces, "Understanding the role of mortality credits"; Milevsky on Yaari (1965), "my lunch with Professor Menahem Yaari"; the "Scott 2008" attribution was not found and was dropped

Kitces's example: a ladder supports about $57.43 a year per $1,000 against about $98.86 from a pooled annuity (25 years, 3%).
critique: Insurer credit risk, fees, no way out. The "collapses to a ladder" step is the scout's inference, not a source's claim.

idea: Brady bonds (1989). Defaulted bank loans were rewritten into bonds whose principal was locked in specially issued 30-year US Treasury zeros held at the New York Fed, while the coupons stayed exposed (some had short rolling guarantees). Ecuador defaulted on its Bradys in 1999; Mexico retired its in 2003.
sources: Wikipedia "Brady Bonds"; Susmel, University of Houston course page (bauer.uh.edu/rsusmel/7386/brady.htm)
use: "The 1989 twin": lock what must not fail in dated Treasuries, let the rest float, and tell the buyer which is which. That is the FINAL's floor fund plus VT, done at national scale, and it justifies stating the bottom and the top at different confidence levels.
critique: The protection was partial and did not prevent later defaults. The vault was bought with borrowed multilateral money. Mathematically it is just a zero plus a risky bond; the novelty was packaging and transparent pricing. The "12-18 month" rolling guarantee is UNVERIFIED. Laura is the investor, not the debtor, and her risky half is shares she owns, with price risk but no default risk.
verified: VERIFIED (S2 via fetch-tool summaries; re-check quotes before citing)
clash: No, provided the FR says Brady's vault was Treasury zeros, which Laura cannot buy (STRIPS are banned). Her vault is coupon bonds and iBonds, which carry reinvestment risk.

idea: The Brady "stripped yield" as a method for the 2031 range. Price the protected principal as a Treasury zero, subtract it, and read the price of risk from what is left. For Laura: strip what is owned (the floor) and quote only the leftover with a probability. Mexican pars' stripped spread went from 254bp (31 Dec 1993) to 452bp (31 Mar 1994).
sources: Susmel, University of Houston course page
use: FR co-sponsor text: quote the bottom as owned and the top as a probability-weighted leftover. Three tools, one range: Brady strips, P99 covers, the newsvendor places.
critique: None beyond row 25

idea: Pitt's sinking fund (1786): £1m a year plus its interest to buy back debt. It worked from 1786 to 1793 while there was a surplus; with war borrowing from 1793 it bought debt with borrowed money. Walpole's earlier fund was raided; Pitt's was abandoned in the 1820s. Robert Hamilton of Aberdeen (1813), not Alexander Hamilton, exposed the fallacy.
sources: Wikipedia "Sinking fund"; Hansard, Commons, 11 Mar 1823 (a cost "equal to a perpetual annuity of 268,000l."; "voted away 324,000,000l."); econbiz full text of The Industrial Revolution (author unconfirmed: the fund "lulled the mind of the ministers"; £271m and £618m borrowed); Wikipedia "Robert Hamilton (economist)"
use: "A promise to save is not a vault": the FINAL buys the payments in January 2027 instead of scheduling savings for them. FR section "what we refused to do". Keel's analogy: paying down a mortgage from a credit card you have not paid off.
critique: The fund was mis-fed, not pointless (the 1823 defenders), so "sinking funds are fraud" is unfair. Price's "penny at the birth of Christ" and Pitt's 1792 rule are UNVERIFIED and dropped. S2 itself notes "the owned bottom is only owned once the 2028 deposit has arrived".
verified: VERIFIED in parts (S2, fetch summaries); part of the Wikipedia date chain is tagged [citation needed]
clash: Partly. S2 says the 2028 money funds "only the floor and the stocks, never the ten payments"; the FINAL says it completes the ladder if yields fall.
where: S2 §2 l.88-148; FUSIONS §2 item 5; README l.72

idea: Ricardo's test: "No sinking fund can be efficient for the purpose of diminishing the debt, if it be not derived from the excess" of revenue over spending. Ask of every dollar the plan counts on: does it exist, or is it promised?
sources: Ricardo, Principles of Political Economy and Taxation, ch. 17 (marxists.org)
use: The $300k exists in January 2027; the 2028 $150k is promised (career income). The honest answer under the FINAL: the ladder is bought with money that exists, and only a gap (if yields fall) waits on the deposit, as its first call.
critique: FUSIONS Conflict 1: the test "tests the 2027 gap". The ladder costs more than $300k in about 47% of paths (MODEL, old design), so the strong form fails.
verified: VERIFIED (quote from the marxists.org text, via S2)
clash: No in the honest form; yes if stated as "no payment waits on money not yet earned".
note: VOID figure (NUMBERS.md 9 Nov): ladder over $300k in about 47% of paths is now $2,287 over at the 6 Nov close (section 1)

idea: Pitt's anti-raid rule. What Pitt got right was making the money hard to raid by law. A stated rule and a public range do the same for Laura against her own future self.
sources: Wikipedia "Sinking fund" (Pitt's 1786 law "stopped ministers from raiding the fund in crises")
use: Backs the FINAL's "only 2 possible reasons we would change our plan" as an anti-raid rule; links to rules over discretion and commitment devices (C R02 47-49).
critique: Pitt's law did not stop the wartime circularity: a rule protects the money only while its source is real.

idea: Perry v. United States (1935). In the one time the US rewrote a bond term (the 1933 gold-clause abrogation), the Court called the abrogation invalid as applied to the bond. But Perry recovered nothing, because he could not show a loss of buying power, so the rewrite stood: "a right with no remedy". The line "as much bound by their contracts as are individuals" is Chief Justice Waite's, from the Sinking-Fund Cases (1879), quoted in Perry.
sources: Cornell LII, 294 U.S. 330; Window 28 Oct correction; FUSIONS header correction (Felix, huddle H-003)
use: Answers "what if the government changes the rules?". The only term ever rewritten was a gold clause, and Laura's bonds are plain dollars. The risk the Court named, buying power, sits on the facility side, which is why the kept half exists. Device: "which clause broke in 1933, and does Laura's bond have one?"
critique: It is a gold-clause case, not about ordinary nominal Treasuries. The "political compromise" reading is UNVERIFIED. It says nothing about debt-ceiling delays (C R02 13). Never write that the Treasury "cannot rewrite a bond", or that terms were "broken": they were "rewritten" once.
verified: VERIFIED (Cornell LII); S2's "cannot rewrite" gloss CONFLICTING (corrected)
clash: No, if worded per the corrections. It supports "barring a US default".

idea: The late Treasury bill payments of April-May 1979: some bill redemptions were paid late. With 1933, these are the only blemishes on the US payment record that the files name.
sources: Felix's correction (huddle H-003); no outside source cited
use: The honest edge of "barring a US default": the near-miss was a delay. That is one more reason each holding matures before its January (C R02 13).
critique: None recorded. It concerns bills, which Laura does not hold directly.

idea: Project-finance two-test sizing. Lenders size debt on both P50 (the expected case, at about 1.20-1.30x DSCR) and P99 (the 1-in-100 bad case, at about 1.00x) and lend the lower amount. Under a normal curve with a 10% standard deviation, P90 is about 87% of P50 and P99 about 77%.
sources: Renewables Valuation Institute, "P50 vs. P99 in Project Finance: How Lenders Size Debt"; Forvis Mazars DSCR page; edbodmer.com wind P99 page (not opened)
use: How to state two numbers at two confidence levels without contradiction: a floor defensible in the 1-in-100 case, a top defensible in the expected case, and an announced gift equal to the lower of what the two tests allow.
critique: The normal curve ignores fat tails (C R02 59). Wind years are independent and stock years are not, so a 1-in-100 year is not a 1-in-100 path. The multiples are convention. Lenders can walk away; Laura cannot.

idea: The cost-overrun facility and the order of call. A committed pre-completion standby is "callable only after contingency is fully used and contractor obligations are enforced", and the sponsor funds "all or a capped portion" last. Worked example (illustrative): budget 1,000, contingency 70 (7%), facility 100 (10%).
sources: Private Equity Bro, "Cost overrun facilities in project finance"; Gowling, Mondaq and rets.ai pieces not opened
use: The FINAL's kept half ("for building costs that overrun, a stronger Taiwan dollar or a co-sponsor falling short") is a capped standby, called last, after the contractor, insurance, contingency and co-sponsors. Laura's gift is a capped contribution, not a completion undertaking. Say so, because overruns arrive when costs rise (repo check: Taiwan construction cost index +6.53% y/y, Aug 2026).
critique: The contingency size is illustrative, and real overruns are larger (C R05 19). Lenders rarely accept a cap on a completion guarantee. The "cost-to-complete undertaking" label is slightly off.

idea: Contingent support goes uncounted, so price it. "Almost without exception, sponsors' financial reports ignore completion guarantees." Proposed charge = (50% minus P(abandonment)) x mean overrun + P(abandonment) x debt; e.g. a $500m project with $300m debt, a $50m overrun and 1% abandonment gives $27.5m.
sources: IJGlobal, "Quantifying contingent support in project financings"
use: Laura's 2031 range is itself a contingent commitment, and pricing it even roughly is the knowledgeable move for the FR.
critique: One author's proposal, not a standard; the 1% is invented for illustration.

idea: Florence's Monte delle doti (1425). A father deposited money when his daughter was about five, and the fund paid a named sum at marriage after 5-15 years. Depositors were lending to the Commune, which reportedly raided the fund in the 1480s.
sources: Wikipedia "Monte delle doti"; a Unibo article quoting Molho (1994) p.31; Market Histories (a popular site, UNVERIFIED against Molho); Molho, Marriage Alliance in Late Medieval Florence (1994), and Kirshner-Molho (1978), titles only
use: "Same promise, different holder": the instrument has barely changed in 600 years, so what matters is who holds the money. A human story hook for an FR page on why to prefund and why Treasuries.
critique: The payment date was marriage, not fixed, so ages were fudged. The issuer was also the borrower. The return was a lure (11-15%), not a match. A dowry fund had no ladder or matching, so "the same idea" stretches. It had a forfeit feature Laura lacks.
verified: PARTLY; rate CONFLICTING (11-12% against "up to 15%": quote no rate); the 1480s raid UNVERIFIED

idea: Muni escrows and yield burning. Dealers overcharged for the escrow Treasuries in advance refundings. Lehman's 1994 portfolio of $15.8m carried a 0.42% markup, and Lehman agreed to pay $450,151.62 to issuers and $4,520,857.29 to the US Treasury.
sources: SEC administrative proceeding 33-7835
use: "Cover after costs": headroom is only real after execution cost. Illustration: 0.42% of a $298k ladder is about $1,250, about two-thirds of the 16 Oct headroom (MODEL, old design). An FR Articulation footnote on real-world execution.
critique: The cases were about tax-arbitrage rules and dealer conduct, not escrow design. WInS charges a flat $10 per bond trade, with no markup.

idea: The debt service reserve account (DSRA), a cash reserve (usually 6-12 months of debt service) for revenue disruption: seems relevant, isn't, because Laura's ladder has no revenue to disrupt. The nearest real thing is the gap between a bond's maturity and its January payment.
sources: FE Training, "Debt service reserve account"
use: One sentence: the buffer has a name and a convention. The trap: a DSRA is often a letter of credit (someone else's promise), while Laura's vault is a bond.
critique: S2 called the buffer "about two months" (the old November-maturity design). In the locked TNA, the Feb 2037 bond covers the Jan 2038 payment, a 10.5-month gap with its own reinvestment risk.

idea: The DSCR distribution lock-up. Three zones (target, lock-up, default) give warning room before a cliff, e.g. "nothing goes to the facility while funded cover is below the lock-up level".
sources: Forvis Mazars DSCR page (1.30x lock-up and 1.10x default in the worked example)
use: Could make the 2031 gift decision automatic; S2 says fold it into the Courtroom's lock rather than add a rule.
critique: Large overlap with L-10 and the lock. The page warns that the 1.30x sizing target is not a covenant level.
clash: Partly. A cover-triggered rule adds a trigger beyond the FINAL's two reasons; acceptable only if it limits the gift, never the payments.

sources: Forvis Mazars page

A chart can be revised in the quiet phase, and Laura's announced range cannot. Fundraisers say a range invites co-sponsors to plan on the bottom.

sources: S3 #1's chain; FUSIONS §2 item 8; test T6

idea: Rosenwald's seed, match and sunset. Julius Rosenwald refused a perpetual endowment ("Real endowments are not money, but ideas"), required local communities to match his gifts and funded more than 5,000 one-room schools (4,978 in one exhibit). His fund was spent out in 1948, about a decade before its deadline.
sources: Wikipedia "Rosenwald Fund"; Philanthropy Roundtable, "Debates on perpetuity" and "Julius Rosenwald's timeless legacy of donor intent"
use: FR facility section: Laura's gift is a dated, capped seed that others match, not an operating endowment, and the cap does the sunsetting.
critique: Philanthropy Roundtable is a donor-intent advocacy group. Matching may favour communities that can already pay (not checked). A residency needs running money after the gift, which Rosenwald's model does not answer.

idea: Tobin's rule against spending down. Trustees are "the guardians of the future against the claims of the present" (preserve real value, keep equity among generations), while spend-down donors give it all within a window. Seems relevant, mostly isn't: Laura's plan spends down by design.
sources: Tobin, "What is Permanent Endowment Income?", American Economic Review 64(2), 1974, quoted in Yale's Principles of Investment Management (lecture pdf)
use: FR "considered and rejected", plus the real-versus-nominal point (row 48).
critique: It assumes an endless life and a real target. Neither side has a clean empirical test.
verified: VERIFIED (quote read in the Yale document, not Tobin's paper)
where: S3 §3 l.119-153; FUSIONS §3 l.158; README l.80

sources: Wikipedia "Atlantic Philanthropies"

idea: Nominal promises owned, real hope in the cushion. Laura's payments are fixed nominal dollars, so at 2.5% inflation (JPM LTCMA) the 2042 payment buys less than the 2033 one. That is the case's design: the plan keeps the nominal promises with certainty and puts any real-value growth in the shares.
sources: S3's reading of Tobin; the JPM LTCMA 2.5% inflation figure used in the repo
use: Says exactly what "certainty" covers and what it does not. Matches TNA note 1 ("Laura's payments are fixed in nominal dollars ... we don't need TIPS") and the FINAL's half kept for building costs and the Taiwan dollar.
critique: "Jun would need to model how much" the 2042 payment loses.
verified: Framing; the inflation figure is the repo's verified LTCMA

idea: The waqf: where to put rigidity. The founder's deed fixed the purpose and the rules, and Kuran argues "the system lacked the flexibility to keep up with rapidly changing economic conditions". Be rigid only where certainty is the whole point (the ten payments) and flexible elsewhere (the facility sum, the cushion).
sources: Kuran, "The Provision of Public Goods under Islamic Law: Origins, Impact, and Limitations of the Waqf System", Law & Society Review 35 (2001), pp. 841-843
use: An FR paragraph, "where we put the rigidity": the FINAL fixes the payments and leaves the facility figure open until 2031.
critique: Kuran's rigidity thesis is contested; the same article says founders' directives were "often circumvented".

idea: The Ottoman cash waqfs of Bursa (1555-1823). Founders fixed rates of about 10.8% (1555) to 13% (1823) while market rates ran higher. About 20% survived more than a century, and growing the initial capital was "an important factor"; state policy ended them.
sources: muslimheritage.com, "Ottoman cash waqfs revisited: Bursa" (a heritage-site summary; the original paper was not opened)
use: "Fixed promises survive on growth in the part that is allowed to grow."
critique: No data on capital erosion, inflation or bad debts. How much of the failure was rigidity, trustee self-dealing or the state is unknown.

idea: Taiwan's hui (合會, 標會) and Civil Code Art. 709-5, 709-6, 709-7 and 709-9. The organiser (會首) takes the first pot without bidding, must pay any contribution members fail to pay, and is jointly liable for the payments owed by members who have already won a pot. The custom was codified in 2000.
sources: legis-pedia.com article 902 (a secondary commentary; the Ministry of Justice site refused access); 月旦法學雜誌 No. 243 (2015) abstract at lawdata.com.tw; Besley, Coate and Loury (1993), American Economic Review (LSE summary); Wikipedia "Hui (informal loan club)"
use: A Taiwanese co-sponsor already knows the question to ask of any pooled promise: "who stands behind the last payment?" Laura's answer is a hui whose organiser is the US Treasury. The shares are where an organiser could come up short, which is why they are never promised. Laura is the last seat in the circle.
critique: A hui is a credit club, not an investment. Its payments rotate between people, while Laura's go one way. There are no sources for Taiwan bid rates or losses (Wikipedia's collapse examples are Vietnamese). Wharton judges may not know it.
verified: VERIFIED through secondary sources (Art. 709-1 not retrieved)

idea: Ergodicity and gambler's ruin: an average across many investors hides the fact that one investor taking a fixed $50k a year out of shares can run dry, and no later good year brings back a missed payment. So payment safety has to be built in (structural), not left to the odds (statistical).
sources: Peters, "The ergodicity problem in economics", Nature Physics 15 (2019) (coin toss: +50%/-40%; positive average, negative typical path); Doctor, Wakker and Wang, Nature Physics 2020 rebuttal (Tinbergen summary); Wikipedia "Gambler's ruin" (Pascal to Fermat, 1656); Milevsky and Robinson, "A Sustainable Spending Rate without Simulation", FAJ 2005
niche: NICHE (ergodicity framing); gambler's ruin is TEXTBOOK
use: "Laura's wealth grows by multiplication but her payments leave in fixed dollars; the only safe way out is to fix it in dollars with instruments that pay in dollars." Coin toss: the average investor gains, the typical one loses.
critique: Peters is contested ("elementary misunderstandings") and partly restates Kelly/log utility (R02 #34); cite him only with the rebuttal. Ruin here is finite (ten payments) and binary (a broken promise). Scout toy model (ILLUSTRATIVE, MODEL (old design), all-stock, JPM 6.7%/16.47%): about 13% of paths miss a payment (24% under 2 pt stress) while mean terminal wealth is about $0.76m and the median about $0.50m.
verified: VERIFIED by S4 (Nature abstract and commented copy; Wikipedia; Milevsky abstract only). RG1's "1654" is CONFLICTING (1656).
where: S4 §2 (l.73-118); RG1 [12] gambler's ruin, ergodicity (l.124, l.126)

idea: Allais and the certainty effect: people give up a lot of expected value for a sure thing. Laura's ten payments are her stated "sure thing" (the case requires it; it's not a taste). The plan is the Allais pattern made consistent: one certain pot and one gamble pot. The twist: certainty costs Laura almost nothing, because the Treasury curve prices the ladder fairly and the unpromised money still buys shares.
sources: Tversky and Kahneman, "Prospect Theory", Econometrica 1979; Wikipedia "Allais paradox" (Allais, Paris conference 1952; Econometrica 1953); R06 D4 (repo: "certainty costs Laura about nothing")
niche: KNOWN (Allais is TEXTBOOK in decision theory; the "hers is cheap" twist is NICHE)
use: "The usual price of certainty is large; hers is small." For the FR's answer to the sceptic.
critique: The paradox describes behaviour, it doesn't justify it ("a bias, not an argument"). Its probabilities are cleaner than any portfolio's. Judges know the certainty effect as a flaw; the reply is that a missed payment is a broken promise, a cliff that dollars don't capture. Savage's own answers UNVERIFIED.
verified: VERIFIED by S4 (K&T abstract page; Wikipedia). The R06 D4 cost-of-certainty figure is MODEL (old design) and must be re-run on the FINAL plan.

idea: Contingent immunisation run backwards: CI manages a portfolio actively and locks in a floor only when the cushion runs out. idea: Bullet vs barbell (Fong-Vasicek): bonds that all mature at the payment date (a bullet) deliver in every case. Test risk payment by payment, not by the whole book's "10-year duration".
sources: Fong and Vasicek, "The Tradeoff between Return and Risk in Immunized Portfolios", FAJ 1983; Fabozzi textbook tradition (RG1); R02 #10, R05 #7

critique: Low novelty; overlaps R02 #10 and R05 #7. Scout zero-coupon toy (ILLUSTRATIVE, MODEL (old design), late-Sep 2026 curve 2y 4.81/5y 4.98/10y 5.17): the barbell gains about 0.4-0.5% on a 1 pt parallel move and loses 1.4-3.1% on a twist; on a "$150k floor" a 2% twist is about $3k.

idea: Two-sided refutation: name the strongest objection a professional would raise and answer it in the same text. That beats a one-sided case; naming an objection and leaving it unanswered is worse than silence.

idea: Swiss cheese and common-cause failure: count failures by cause, not by component. Laura's layers (the reinvested coupons, the 2028 deposit, the share cushion) may share one hole: a recession that lowers yields, cuts her writing income and drops shares all at once. R11 L4 adds that held-to-maturity bonds don't mind falling prices; their only weakness is yields falling for good, which usually comes with the same slump. A 2022-style year (yields up, shares down) opens a different pair of holes.

idea: Uncertainty about how much is needed breaks group funding; uncertainty about the size of the benefit does not. Threshold known: catastrophe avoided in 18 of 20 groups (8/10 with known impact, 10/10 with uncertain impact). Threshold uncertain: catastrophe certain in 16 of 20 groups and at least 80% likely in the other 4

critique: A climate game with 10 equal players avoiding a loss; the facility cost itself stays uncertain and is outside scope (case p.4)
clash: no; supports FLOOR and MOVE2031. TNA l.21 (D4): before the move the top moves, so a co-sponsor who plans on the top faces a moving threshold
note: Top-40: in the lab, groups funded a known threshold 18 times in 20 and an uncertain one never; the owned floor and the 2031 move take Laura's part of that uncertainty away.

idea: The width of the uncertainty has a sharp cut-off: threshold known at 150, 80% of groups avoided catastrophe; uncertain over 100-200, 135-165 or 140-160, none did; over 145-155, 40% did. A later replication: 90% vs 42%, and a warning that narrowed the uncertainty to within 10% raised it to 61%
sources: Barrett, S. & Dannenberg, A. (2014) "Sensitivity of collective action to uncertainty about climate tipping points", Nature Climate Change 4: 36-39, as reported in Hurlstone et al. (2025), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11898102
use: The cut-off lies between ranges about 7% and 13% of the threshold wide (Keel arithmetic: 10/150 and 20/150); narrow beats wide by far more than intuition suggests
critique: The 2014 numbers read only in a secondary account; lab climate games
verified: VERIFIED: Hurlstone et al. 2025 full text; Barrett & Dannenberg 2014 UNVERIFIED at source
note: A sharp cut-off in tolerable uncertainty, but the 2014 figures were read only in a secondary account.

idea: Ambiguity (an unknown spread) is worse than known risk, and "Early and credible commitment helps groups to cope with uncertainty"; in theory more ambiguity lowers the largest number of contributors

(2015) "On the provision of public goods with probabilistic and ambiguous thresholds", Environmental and Resource Economics 61(3): 365-383, https://researchonline.lse.ac.uk/id/eprint/57121/ ; Kishishita, D. & Ozaki, H. (2020) "Public goods game with ambiguous threshold", Economics Letters 191, https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/ecolet/v191y2020ics0165176520301282.html

critique: Lab and theory

idea: The counter-case: in theory, when a good is valued highly, wider threshold uncertainty can raise contributions because each giver feels more likely to be the one who tips it; the lab gave "only limited verification", and wider uncertainty "will sometimes, but not always," hinder collective action

(2010) "Threshold uncertainty in discrete public good games: an experimental study", Economics of Governance 11(1): 77-99, https://escholarship.org/uc/item/49p8c2jv

idea: The uncertainty effect: people value a risky prospect below its worst outcome (over 1,000 participants); a replication put it at about 65% of the worse outcome, shown by at least 62% of people
sources: Gneezy, U., List, J.A. & Wu, G. (2006) "The uncertainty effect: when a risky prospect is valued less than its worst possible outcome", QJE 121(4): 1283-1309, https://academic.oup.com/qje/article-abstract/121/4/1283/1855222 ; Simonsohn, U. (2009) "Direct risk aversion: evidence from risky prospects valued below their worst outcome", Psychological Science 20(6): 686-692, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19422629
use: A bare range can be valued below its own bottom; a bottom presented as owned money gives the listener a sure thing to anchor on (Keel inference)
critique: Contested: Keren & Willemsen (2009, JBDM 22: 301-317) found it nearly vanished with clear instructions; Rydval et al. (2009, Experimental Economics 12: 473-487) questioned it; neither read at source
verified: VERIFIED: QJE and PubMed abstracts; critiques UNVERIFIED
note: The uncertainty effect is contested by later studies that were not read; cite only with the doubt stated.

idea: People use risk "as an excuse not to give": when money for themselves is traded against money for a charity, a risky impact lowers giving more than it should
sources: Exley, C.L. (2016) "Excusing selfishness in charitable giving: the role of risk", Review of Economic Studies 83(2): 587-628, https://www.hbs.edu/ris/Publication%20Files/Excusing%20Selfishness_Published_d8e096a8-ca8c-42ed-a8d4-f3b0b993ded1.pdf

critique: Individuals in a lab; institutional budgets follow other rules

idea: In US nonprofit accounting a "condition" needs both a barrier for the recipient and a right of return or release; a market-set top has neither, so it is not a condition but an amount not yet promised

FASB. 958-605-25-5A: "A donor-imposed condition must have both"; 25-5B: "it must be determinable from the agreement (or another document referenced in the agreement)". https://storage.fasb.org/ASU%202018-08.pdf
use: The bottom can be booked as an unconditional promise; the top before the move is booked as nothing, so "conditional up to" is the wrong label for it (Keel inference)

idea: Commitment words decide whether a pledge exists: "Words such as 'promise,' 'pledge,' and 'agree' may indicate a commitment, while 'plan' or 'intend' may suggest only a potential gift"; "An oral promise may also qualify if adequately documented and verifiable"

critique: An accounting firm's guidance, not the standard; the standard's own documentation paragraph not read at source
note: 3d: commitment verbs decide whether a pledge exists ('promise' for the minimum, 'plan' for the band), and the IPS's verbs already fit.

idea: The same promise shows two numbers: books measure unconditional pledges "at fair value" and discount longer-term ones "to present value"; campaign counting reports pledges "at face value"

idea: A pledge made conditional on a match "should not be counted until the institution has fulfilled the terms of the match"

idea: Numbers cost less trust than words: numeric uncertainty cut trust in the number by d = -0.15 and verbal uncertainty by d = -0.55; on trust in the source the effects were d = -0.03 (not significant) and d = -0.21; the authors recommend "numerical ranges with a point estimate" (a range without one lowered trust in the number in Experiment 3)
sources: van der Bles, A. M., van der Linden, S., Freeman, A. L. J., & Spiegelhalter, D. J. (2020). The effects of communicating uncertainty on public trust in facts and numbers. *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 117*(14), 7672-7683. https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1913678117
use: State the range in numbers with a central figure; words such as "around" without numbers are the costly form
critique: Facts about the present, read by the public, not promises read by funders
clash: no; a central figure is a writing choice, not a plan change
where: This run; adds effect sizes to Q11a row 31
note: 3c: numbers cost little trust (d = -0.15) and words much more (d = -0.55), best as a range with a central figure; stronger than Q11a-031, which a later pass should merge into this row.

idea: People do not dislike uncertain advice, only advisers who sound unsure; ranges and probabilities were not penalised (11 studies, N = 4,806): "Advisors benefit from expressing themselves with confidence, but not from communicating false certainty"
sources: Gaertig, C., & Simmons, J. P. (2018). Do people inherently dislike uncertain advice? *Psychological Science, 29*(4), 504-520. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29466077
use: A stated probability is safe; "we are not sure" is not
critique: Forecasts of events by lay advisers, not funders
note: 3c: people accept uncertain advice but not advisers who sound unsure, so state the confidence plainly.

idea: Quantified ranges have null or small effects; disagreement framing is the costly kind: "quantified error ranges and probabilities (technical uncertainty) ... has had only positive or null effects, not negative effects" (k = 48); technical uncertainty d = -0.15 on attitudes, none on credibility (43 articles); "no overall effect" on trust (28 studies); uncertainty raised trust and donation intention (N = 88)
sources: Gustafson, A., & Rice, R. E. (2020). A review of the effects of uncertainty in public science communication. *Public Understanding of Science*; Guo, Z., et al. (2025). A meta-analysis synthesizing the effects of three uncertainty types in science communication. *Science Communication*; Dries, C., et al. (2026). The impact of uncertainty communication on trust in its sources: A systematic review and meta-analysis. *Royal Society Open Science*; Steijaert, M., et al. (2020). Two-sided science. *Communications*. Abstract pages: https://consensus.app/papers/details/e1d4bda6eed856b28a95e6e301a90c48/ ; https://consensus.app/papers/details/866c2359099e5514a7a5077e0d29fca2/ ; https://consensus.app/papers/details/74b8c3f387d1570e83d88b1df9c42612/ ; https://consensus.app/papers/details/68d05a27c6fd5a6aa3d9513895105f51/
use: Present one team range, not rival forecasts that read as disagreement
critique: Science-news readers; Steijaert's sample is small
note: 3c: quantified ranges cost nothing on average and disagreement framing does, so present one team range, not rival forecasts.

idea: A stated uncertainty cushions trust when the facts later change: "communicating uncertainty buffers against a loss of trust when evidence changes" (N = 800)
sources: Dries, C., et al. (2024). When evidence changes: Communicating uncertainty protects against a loss of trust. *Public Understanding of Science*. Abstract page: https://consensus.app/papers/details/56a2f293df3e5e07810807c126782faf/
use: If 2033 lands differently from 2031's picture, an earlier stated range protects Laura's standing

note: 3c: a range stated in advance cushions trust if 2033 differs from 2031's picture; one study.

A., & MacCoun, R. J. (2013). Cheap talk and credibility. *Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 121*(2), 246-255. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S074959781300023X

verified: VERIFIED (summary sheet and Part 1, ch. 1 to 3, read); ch. 8 UNVERIFIED
note: Same Few look-up point as Q23-022; adds 'combine summary and detail in a single display' for Table 1's one subtotal.

idea: IBTM does two jobs: the 2033 payment and the floor; in the WInS book it is one row, $97,489.95, 32.50% (8g). A role grouping cannot split one holding into two rows within Wharton's one row per holding
sources: TNA l.13 ("IBTM does two jobs"); CANON A24, D2; NUMBERS 8g
use: The only role group that fits is the Treasuries "for the ten payments and the floor" ($268,652.18, 89.55%, 8g); the table note names IBTM's two jobs as the TNA does
critique: None
clash: risk: a group named for the payments alone would contradict the submitted Trading Note on IBTM
note: Table 1: IBTM does two jobs (TNA), so one subtotal under the ten Treasuries 'for the ten payments and the floor' ($268,652.18, 89.55%, NUMBERS 8g); a group named for the payments alone would contradict the Trading Note.

idea: Rounding Table 1 costs nothing: the 8g amounts rounded to whole dollars still sum to exactly $300,000, and the percentages to one decimal still sum to exactly 100.0 (own arithmetic on 8g, not a new figure); Wharton's own example row is in whole dollars and whole %
sources: NUMBERS 8g; WHARTON_NORTH_STAR s. 0 example row
use: Wainer and Ehrenberg's rounding (rows 27, 28) fits Wharton's totals exactly; it also narrows the amount column
critique: specs.md keeps cents and two decimals; the register stays in cents either way
note: Table 1 option, checked: 8g rounded to whole dollars and one-decimal % still totals $300,000 and 100.0%; SKELETON keeps cents and two decimals as WInS records them.

idea: The May-2038 bond's waiting time is "7.6 months" in NUMBERS 8h and specs, "7.5 months" in the submitted trade note; CANON B35 rates 7.5 TRUE as rounding (231 days)
sources: CANON A16, B35; NUMBERS 8h; specs.md Figure 1 Form row
use: Figure 1's label should read 7.5 months, so a judge who read the trade note sees the same number
critique: 7.6 is the more exact figure; both are honest
clash: risk: "7.6 months" on Figure 1 beside "7.5 months" in the Trading Notes reads as a mismatch across deliverables judged together
note: Figure 1's label says '7.5 months' for the May-2038 bond, matching the submitted trade note (CANON A16, B35), not the register's 7.6.

idea: US foundation giving ROSE in the crash year: foundation assets fell 17.2% in 2008 ($682.2bn to $565.0bn) while foundation giving rose 5.4% ($44.4bn to $46.8bn). The yearbook says funders cut operating costs or drew on endowments to "shore up" giving, and used "asset-averaging"
sources: Foundation Center, Foundations Today Series 2010, "Foundation Growth and Giving Estimates" highlights, https://www.giarts.org/sites/default/files/Foundation_Growth_2010.pdf ; second copy https://carolinapublicpress.org/wp-content/uploads/2012/01/Foundation-Center-2010-yearbook.pdf (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: A foundation's grant budget for a year is mostly set before the crash. Shares fall first and grants follow later
critique: US foundations only. Part of the 2008 rise is Gates (row 31) and gifts still arriving. 2008 grants were largely committed in 2007
clash: yes, partly: the IPS says co-sponsors cut "during that same period" as shares fall; for foundations the cut comes a year or more later (risk to note)
note: Top-40 candidate: US foundation giving rose 5.4% in 2008 as foundation assets fell 17.2%; grants follow assets late, so the IPS's 'same period' needs the lag.

idea: The counted 2009 fall was small. Foundation giving fell 2.1% to $45.8bn in 2009 (a "record" decline) and 0.2% to $45.7bn in 2010. The first estimate had been -8.4% (Foundation Center 2010), Giving USA 2010 printed -8.9% current, and the 2009 forecast was -8% to -13%
sources: Foundation Center, Foundations Today Series 2011 highlights, https://carolinapublicpress.org/wp-content/uploads/2012/01/Foundation-Center-yearbook-2011.pdf ; Foundations Today 2009 edition highlights, https://search.issuelab.org/resource/foundations-today-foundation-yearbook-2009-edition-highlights ; row 1 URL (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: Peak to trough, US foundation giving fell about 2.3% ($46.8bn to $45.7bn, Keel arithmetic) while the S&P 500 fell 36.55%
critique: Nominal: the real fall is a little larger. Only one crash. Estimates made during a crash overstate the fall
verified: VERIFIED (both highlights PDFs). CORRECTS store H9-013, whose "foundation giving fell 8.6% in 2009 (8.9% current)" is the early estimate
note: The counted 2009 foundation fall was 2.1%, not the early 8-9% estimates; corrects H9-013.

idea: By type in 2009: independent foundations -3.2%, community foundations -7.1%, corporate foundations +2.6% (after +3.9% in 2008), and the 25 largest funders +14.2%. The reasons given are "the commitment of many foundations to maintaining their grants budgets or reducing the extent of reductions relative to their assets losses", a market rebound, and new foundations
sources: Foundation Center 2011 highlights (row 2 URL); 2008 corporate figure from the 2010 highlights (row 1 URL) (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: For a co-sponsor list: big endowed funders and corporate foundations held up best in 2009, and community foundations cut most
critique: A corporate foundation (with its own endowment) is not the same as a company's giving budget (rows 15-16). US only
note: Big endowed and corporate foundations held up best in 2009 and community foundations cut most.

idea: Foundations spent a larger share of their assets in the crash. The median payout rate of 979 endowed foundations was 5.4% (2007), 5.8% (2008) and 6.4% (2009) while their assets fell about 24% in 2008. The 2009 yearbook names "short-term increases in payout rates" and a "rolling average of their asset values"
sources: Foundation Center, "Foundation Payout" (2012), https://foundationcenter.issuelab.org/resources/14076/14076.pdf ; 2009 highlights (row 2 URL) (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: Smoothing is why the lag exists: grants follow an average of past asset values, not this year's price
critique: A higher rate on a smaller base still means smaller grants a year or two later
note: Foundations smooth grants on average past asset values, which is why the lag exists.

idea: US law builds in the lag. The 5% minimum is figured on asset values set "on a monthly basis" over the year. A foundation has until the end of the following year to pay it before a 30% tax, and excess payouts carry forward
sources: 26 U.S. Code s 4942, https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/4942 (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: A crash in one year lowers the required grants mostly in the next two years, so a US foundation met in 2031 pays a 2033 pledge partly from earlier, higher asset values
critique: US private foundations only. The rule is a floor and many pay more. Taiwan's rules for foundations were not checked (gap)
verified: VERIFIED (statute text); the lag in years is Keel inference
where: This run: Cornell LII statute page
note: US payout law builds in a lag of up to two years; Taiwan rules not checked.

idea: Community foundations kept granting while gifts into them fell: grants were up 15% on 2006 while gifts received were down 22% (2009 survey)
sources: Council on Foundations, 2009 Columbus Survey results, https://cof.org/sites/default/files/2023-08/04-08-10_2009%20Columbus%20Survey%20Results_29221_0.pdf (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: Pass-through funders run down their balances to keep grants up for a year or two
critique: Partly at odds with row 3 (-7.1% in 2009 against 2008); different base year and sample
note: Conflicts with Q4b-003 on a different base year; do not use either figure alone.

idea: 2022, the last big share fall: the S&P 500 fell 19.4% (-25.4% real). Foundation giving rose 2.5% to $105.21bn (-5.0% real), corporate giving rose 3.4% to $29.48bn (-4.2% real), individuals fell 6.4% (-13.4% real), and arts giving rose 2.9% current
sources: Giving USA 2023 press release, Indiana University Lilly Family School of Philanthropy, https://news.iu.edu/philanthropy/live/news/51591-giving-usa-total-us-charitable-giving-declined-in (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: When shares fell alongside high inflation, institutional givers held their budgets in money terms, and their real cuts were small
critique: One year. Inflation, not the market, did most of the real cut
note: In the 2022 share fall institutional givers held their budgets in money terms.

idea: The lag year after 2022: foundation giving fell 2.3% real in 2023, to $103.53bn from $105.99bn (2023 dollars). 22% of foundations cut their payout rate in 2022, and for 2023 more expected to cut (27%) than raise (23%), the first time in the survey's history. 79% of 546 said inflation did not change their 2022 grants, several because grants "are based on the average market return of assets over multiple years"
sources: Giving USA 2024 via BWF, https://www.bwf.com/giving-usa-2024-report-insights/ ; Candid, https://candid.org/blogs/foundation-giving-and-payout-in-2022-what-changed-whats-next ; https://candid.org/blogs/how-inflation-affects-grantmaking-decisions-foundations ; https://candid.org/blogs/foundation-giving-data-in-2023-expected-grantmaking-in-2024 ; Chronicle of Philanthropy, 29 Jun 2023, https://www.philanthropy.com/news/many-foundations-are-taking-a-step-back-after-2-years-of-steep-increases-in-grants-budgets (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: The foundation cut came one year after the share fall, while shares were recovering. This is the same shape as 2008-09
critique: Candid's own sample shows 2023 grants up 1.7% ($25.8bn to $26.2bn; median +0.3%; median payout of independent foundations 5%, mean 7.5%). Giving USA's real figure and Candid's nominal figure differ
verified: CONFLICTING on size (Giving USA -2.3% real; Candid sample +1.7% nominal); timing agrees
where: This run: BWF page, Candid blogs, Chronicle article
note: Sources disagree on the size of the 2023 cut; only the one-year timing agrees.

idea: Arts giving held through the 2022 share fall. In 2023 dollars, arts, culture and humanities giving was $23.55bn (2019), $22.70bn (2020), $23.49bn (2021), $23.70bn (2022) and $25.26bn (2023, +6.6% real)
sources: Giving USA 2024 table as given by BWF, https://www.bwf.com/giving-usa-2024-report-insights/ (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: The worst recent year for US arts giving was the 2020 shutdown (-3.6% real, Keel arithmetic), not the 2022 share fall
critique: US totals, mostly from individuals. This is not building co-sponsorship. Read through BWF, not the Giving USA report
verified: VERIFIED (BWF's table); Giving USA report itself not read
note: US arts giving held through 2022 and its worst recent year was the 2020 shutdown; read via BWF.

idea: Foundations do not act counter-cyclically. Their payouts after financial shocks show "retrenchment" or "independence", not more giving when need rises
sources: Calabrese, T.D. & Ely, T.L. (2022) "How US Private Foundations Change Payouts Based on Financial Shocks: Revealed Publicness or Revealed Privateness?", Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory 32(1): 166-182, https://academic.oup.com/jpart/article/32/1/166/6277840 (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: Do not assume a foundation co-sponsor will step in when others cut
critique: US data. Abstract only
note: Foundations do not step up when need rises; abstract only.

idea: Foundations respond asymmetrically. "A 10 percent asset shock raises payout rates by 10 to 16 basis points for positive returns but decreases them by 31 to 39 basis points after negative returns". They "do not increase aggregate spending in periods of elevated need". Founder-family foundations cut 102% more after losses. Peers crowd each other out (elasticity -0.22). Median grant payout is 4.84%, and the correlation between foundations' returns is 0.44
sources: Lu, Y. & Malliaris, S. (2026) "Charitable capital allocation: Evidence from private foundations", Journal of Financial Economics 185, 104377 (open access), https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0304405X26001480 (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: Foundations still run by the founder's family are the likeliest to cut. Because their returns move together, shortfalls tend to come in clusters
critique: Rates, not dollars. In 2008-09 the aggregate rate rose (row 4) because grants lagged falling assets. US only
clash: yes, partly: supports the cluster risk in Q9 row 30 (risk to note)
note: Founder-family foundations cut most after losses and foundations' returns move together, so co-sponsor shortfalls can cluster; a risk to note.

idea: University endowments cut payouts below their own policy after losses but do not raise them after gains ("endowment hoarding"). A later study found symmetric responses
sources: Brown, J.R., Dimmock, S.G., Kang, J.-K. & Weisbenner, S.J. (2014) "How University Endowments Respond to Financial Market Shocks", American Economic Review 104(3), https://consensus.app/papers/details/7831f601f303581cb3e87906847e0fab/ ; Rosen et al. (2019), Journal of Higher Education (via Consensus search) (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: A partner university or other endowed body protects its endowment first
critique: Universities, not arts funders
note: Two studies disagree on whether endowments cut asymmetrically; low direct use.

idea: Million-dollar gifts from foundations "tend to be countercyclical". Corporate million-dollar giving is less tied to the economy. Million-dollar gifts to the arts go with good economic conditions
sources: Osili, U. et al. (2018) "Economic Effects on Million Dollar Giving", Nonprofit and Voluntary Sector Quarterly, https://consensus.app/papers/details/d558d16e83195cf6b31f8d6f98a7f6b8/ (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: Big single grants from foundations may be the steadiest co-sponsor money. Big arts gifts from individuals are the least steady
critique: US. Abstract only
note: Big single foundation gifts may be the steadiest co-sponsor money; abstract only.

idea: Donations respond more to booms than to busts (US aggregate data, 1968-2007)
sources: List, J.A. & Peysakhovich, Y. (2011) "Charitable donations are more responsive to stock market booms than busts", Economics Letters, https://consensus.app/papers/details/a1e6b1a3c8aa562990811edb9db34cf9/ (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: For all giving, the fall in a crash is milder than the rise in a boom. This matches rows 1-2
critique: Mostly individuals. For foundations the opposite asymmetry is found (row 11)
note: Giving rises more in booms than it falls in busts; mostly individuals.

idea: In the Great Recession, giving fell more than shocks to income or wealth explain; attitudes changed
sources: Meer, J., Miller, D.H. & Wulfsberg, E. (2017) "The Great Recession and charitable giving", Applied Economics Letters, https://consensus.app/papers/details/1142ead87f7951f5ac624ebb5bf70307/ (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: A crash can cut giving through mood as well as money, so a co-sponsor's balance sheet is not the whole story
critique: Household (PSID) data, not institutions
note: Giving fell more than income in the Great Recession, through mood as well as money.

idea: Corporate giving follows profits, not share prices, and the previous year's profits at that. "Corporate giving is tied more closely to corporate profits than stock market performance". Giving as a share of the previous year's pre-tax profit was 1.02% (2007/2006), 0.99% (2008/2007) and 1.21% (2009/2008), and "previous-year profit is related to current-year giving"
sources: Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond, Econ Focus Q2 2010, https://www.richmondfed.org/-/media/RichmondFedOrg/publications/research/econ_focus/2010/q2/pdf/feature3.pdf ; CECP, Giving in Numbers 2010, https://intranet.americansforthearts.org/sites/default/files/GivinginNumbers2010.pdf (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: A corporate co-sponsor's 2033 budget is set from its 2032 profits, which builds in a one-year lag
critique: Large US companies (CECP members)
note: Corporate giving follows last year's profits, a built-in one-year lag; a timing clash with 'same period' to note.

idea: Corporate giving held in 2008, fell in 2009, and switched from cash to goods. Giving rose or held for 63% of companies in 2007-08 while profits fell; it fell for 57-59% in 2009. Cash giving was $4.63bn (2007), $4.53bn (2008) and $4.29bn (2009) for 96 firms (-7.3% over two years, Keel arithmetic). "Many companies compensated for fewer cash grants with product donations". Giving USA: corporate giving rose 5.5% in 2009, driven by in-kind gifts
sources: CECP Giving in Numbers 2012, https://cecp.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/GIN2012_finalweb.pdf ; 2013, https://www.americansforthearts.org/sites/default/files/GIN2013_Web_Final.pdf ; 2010 (row 16 URL); Giving USA 2010 Executive Summary, https://www.americansforthearts.org/sites/default/files/GivingUSA_2010_ExecSummary.pdf (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: In a downturn a corporate co-sponsor may offer materials, equipment or services instead of cash. That helps a residency but does not fill a cash pledge
critique: Large US companies. The arts share in GIN 2013 fell through smaller gifts; the exact share was not captured
where: This run: CECP PDFs, Giving USA summary
note: Corporate cash giving fell in 2009 and shifted to goods, which do not fill a cash pledge; a timing clash to note.

idea: Business support for the arts fell 14% from 2006 to 2009. The share of businesses giving to any cause fell from 70% to 52%, and to the arts from 43% to 28%. Arts sponsorship dollars rose slightly in 2009 but fell after inflation, and the arts' share of sponsorship fell from 6% to 5%
sources: Business Committee for the Arts 2010 survey, as reported by Americans for the Arts, https://intranet.americansforthearts.org/sites/default/files/pdf/get_involved/advocacy/research/2011/business_support11.pdf (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: After a crash, fewer companies give to the arts at all. The pool narrows; the cheques do not just shrink
critique: Survey design and firm sizes not checked
note: After a crash fewer companies give to the arts at all; a timing clash to note.

idea: UK business money for culture fell four years running while trusts and foundations rose. Business: £157m (2008/09, -6%), £144.1m (2009/10, -12%; Third Sector says -11%), £134.2m (2010/11, -7%, "fourth consecutive annual fall", below 2004/05). Trusts and foundations: £135m (2008/09, -7%), £154.6m (2009/10, +11%), £170.3m (2010/11, +10%). Individuals: £382.2m (2010/11, +6%). "Corporate money is a discretionary spend". In 2009 Arts & Business warned "the worst may be yet to come, with 2010-11 being the low-point"
sources: Arts & Business figures via WalesOnline, https://www.walesonline.co.uk/business/business-news/arts-picture-private-investors-wales-1939961 ; Museums Association, 2011, https://www.museumsassociation.org/museums-journal/news/2011/02/01032011-coprorate-giving-to-museums-falls/ and 2012, https://www.museumsassociation.org/museums-journal/news/2012/02/28022012-corporate-giving-falls/ ; Third Sector, https://www.thirdsector.co.uk/corporate-giving-arts-down-11-per-cent/fundraising/article/1051947 ; A&B Private Investment in Culture 2010/11, https://www.leanarts.org.uk/app/uploads/artsandbusiness-private-investment-in-culture10-11.pdf (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: Over 2008/09 to 2010/11, business money fell 14.5% and trusts and foundations rose 26% (nominal, Keel arithmetic). Corporate arts money hit bottom two to three years after the share trough, the longest lag here, while a mix of funder types offset part of it
critique: UK only, one cycle. A&B's percentages may be real while the £ figures are nominal. Read through press reports, except the 2010/11 growth table (business: rise, fall, fall, fall, fall; trusts and foundations: rise, rise, fall, rise, rise; 2006/07 to 2010/11)
verified: VERIFIED (press reports and the A&B 2010/11 table)
clash: yes, partly: the IPS's "during that same period" does not fit a cut that lasted until 2011 (risk to note)
where: This run: news pages and A&B PDF
note: UK business money for culture bottomed two to three years after the share low while trusts rose; press reports; a timing clash to note.

idea: Match money softened the fall. Scotland's £1-for-£1 incentive limited the sponsorship fall to 7% over 2009-10, against 17% for the UK
sources: Culture & Business Scotland, https://cultureandbusiness.scot/new-figures-for-private-investment-in-culture-reveal-contrasting-fortunes-for-the-arts-world (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: Laura's committed lead gift works a little like match money: co-sponsors giving alongside a fixed lead may cut less
critique: One programme. The match effect on Laura is Keel inference
where: This run: Culture & Business Scotland page
note: Match money softened the fall in Scotland; the link to Laura's lead gift is inference.

idea: US federal arts money first rose and was cut later. NEA appropriations: $144.7m (2008), $155.0m (2009, plus $50m Recovery Act money), $167.5m (2010), $154.69m (2011), $146.0m (2012), $138.4m (2013, sequestration), which is -17.4% from 2010 to 2013 (Keel arithmetic). In the pandemic, the NEA received $75m (CARES, 2020) and $135m (ARP, 2021)
sources: National Endowment for the Arts, Appropriations History, https://www.arts.gov/about/appropriations-history (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: Public money can rise in a crash through stimulus, then be cut two to four years later in austerity, after shares have recovered
critique: US federal. This is politics, not markets. Recovery Act money is not in the yearly figures
note: US federal arts money rose in the crash and was cut two to four years later; a timing clash to note.

idea: US state arts agencies cut deepest and latest. Legislative appropriations: $354.1m (FY2008), $328.8m (FY2009), $291.8m (FY2010), $272.6m (FY2011), $260.2m (FY2012, "a low point"), $277.8m (FY2013), $306.5m (FY2014), $350.6m (FY2015). That is -26.5% over FY2008-12 (Keel arithmetic; NASAA says 27%). FY2012 is the year to June 2012, about three years after the March 2009 share low. The earlier cycle ran from $449.5m (FY2001) to $279.9m (FY2004), -37.7%
sources: NASAA, FY2016 revenues news release, https://www.nasaa-arts.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/01/NASAAFY2016SAARevenuesPressRelease.pdf ; FY2016 report, https://www.nasaa-arts.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/NASAAFY2016SAARevenuesReport.pdf ; FY2026 report, https://www.nasaa-arts.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/FY2026-State-Arts-Agency-Revenues-Report_final-updated.pdf (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: A public arts budget is the latest and deepest cutter: it falls for about three years after shares bottom and takes about six years to come back
critique: US states, driven by tax revenue, not share prices
note: Public arts budgets cut deepest and latest, about three years after shares bottomed; a timing clash to note.

idea: NASAA says why: "a built-in recovery time lag: due to the structure of public finances, state budgets take longer to rebound". After the early-1990s and early-2000s recessions, "the decrease in SAA appropriations continued several years after the recession had ended". FY2017 was still 6.7% below FY2008 in real terms. The early 2010 snapshot: state arts appropriations -10%, local government support -8%, private giving to the arts -6.5% (Americans for the Arts testimony). GIA: 2010 state -6.9%, local -8.1%, NEA up
sources: NASAA FY2017 report, https://www.nasaa-arts.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/NASAA-FY2017-SAA-Revenues-Report.pdf ; Americans for the Arts testimony, 13 Apr 2010, https://www.americansforthearts.org/sites/default/files/pdf/news/press/RobertLynch_AADTestimony.pdf ; Grantmakers in the Arts, "Public Funding for the Arts: 2010 Update", https://www.giarts.org/article/public-funding-arts-2010-update (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: Three cycles have had the same shape: public arts money keeps falling after the recession ends
critique: The testimony's line that arts groups run about "a year behind business trends" was seen only in part (UNVERIFIED wording)
verified: VERIFIED (NASAA report, testimony figures, GIA page)
where: This run: PDFs and GIA page
note: Three cycles show public arts money falling after recessions end; a timing clash to note.

idea: Taiwan's corporate arts sponsorship hit a record in the edition covering the crash. The 10th Wenxin Award (文馨獎, 2010) recognised about NT$2.2bn of company giving, the highest of any edition in the award's 12 years (the Executive Yuan, in Chinese) and nearly double the 1st edition's NT$1.15bn. Its 176 winners included 21 that funded rebuilding after Typhoon Morakot. The 16th (2023, covering the pandemic years) recognised NT$1,870,506,685
sources: Executive Yuan news, 7 Aug 2010, https://www.ey.gov.tw/Page/9277F759E41CCD91/600a82fb-fe45-495c-9012-3e600e2cc717 ; NCAF news, 2 Oct 2023, https://www.ncafroc.org.tw/news_detail.html?sid=670 ; rules of the 14th award (two-year counting window, award since 1998, every two years from the 7th), https://www.ncafroc.org.tw/files/official/%E7%AC%AC14%E5%B1%86%E6%96%87%E9%A6%A8%E7%8D%8E%E5%BE%B5%E4%BB%B6%E8%AA%AA%E6%98%8E%E6%9C%83%E7%B0%A1%E5%A0%B1%E8%AA%AA%E6%98%8E.pdf (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: Company money for the arts in Taiwan did not visibly shrink in 2008-09, even with the TAIEX down 46% in 2008
critique: Award totals count only givers who apply and give at least NT$500,000, so this is not a census. That the 10th edition covered 2008-09 is Keel inference from the two-year rule of the 14th. The 9th (2008) total was not found
verified: VERIFIED (EY and NCAF page text, the 14th's rules PDF); window is Keel inference
where: This run: search excerpts of the EY and NCAF pages; rules PDF
note: Taiwan's company arts money did not visibly shrink in 2008-09; award totals are not a census.

idea: Early Wenxin editions recorded corporate arts sponsorship of over NT$1bn every year ("每年皆超過十億元"), so Taiwan's corporate arts money is a steady, sizable pool
sources: 陳以亨, 林瑩滋 & 李星美 (2004) 企業贊助藝文活動的動機因素之研究, 輔仁管理評論 11(1): 33-52, https://www.management.fju.edu.tw/zh-tw/down.php?hFFile=tw_books_caty01331169529.pdf (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: It gives a base for row 24's record. 60% of large firms surveyed had sponsored the arts
critique: Before 2004. Survey of large firms
where: This run: search excerpt of the PDF
note: Taiwan's corporate arts sponsorship has been a steady pool above NT$1bn a year; pre-2004 data.

idea: The cause and year of NCAF's 41% income fall, now settled: 2015, a weak market led by Taiwan shares, after a strong 2014. Financial income was NT$283,520,045 in 2014 (88.9% of revenue) and NT$150,522,150 in 2015. The return was 2.42% against 3.59% expected, with investment losses of NT$75.6m and unrealised losses of NT$173.7m. The TAIEX fell 10.41% in 2015. Total income went from NT$318,803,033 to NT$188,860,003
sources: NCAF Annual Report 2015 (English), https://www.ncafroc.org.tw/files/publishBookEn/20200623/4fa69c5d236e4b53843284ca1e8553fc/4fa69c5d236e4b53843284ca1e8553fc.pdf ; CBC Annual Report 2015, https://www.cbc.gov.tw/en/public/Attachment/661517483371.PDF (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: Taiwan's main public arts grant-maker lives on market returns. Its fund is about NT$2bn each in deposits, shares and fixed income
critique: One foundation. This answers Q9 row 34's critique: 2014 was ordinary investment income, not a one-off
where: This run: NCAF and CBC PDFs

idea: The board that agreed "a serious possibility" of attack in NIE 29-51 meant odds from 20:80 to 80:20; its author meant 65:35

idea: Set in Stone (more than 700 US arts building projects, about $16bn): buildings left "large annual operating expenses that were sometimes beyond the capacity of the organizations that built them", yet "few organizations were actually forced to" close
sources: Woronkowicz, Joynes, Frumkin and others, Set in Stone (University of Chicago Cultural Policy Center, 2012), https://www.norc.org/content/dam/norc-org/pdfs/setinstone%20FINAL%20REPORT.pdf and https://www.drama.yale.edu/app/uploads/2020/04/Set-in-Stone-2012-acs.pdf (accessed 9 Nov 2026)

idea: What decided how groups fared after building was "how flexible and realistic the organization was in projecting revenue for the post-completion period"; those with low fixed costs cut programmes instead of closing
sources: Set in Stone (2012), same URLs: non-resident performing arts centres with low fixed costs closed gaps by presenting fewer shows; museums in trouble cut education programmes; the Taubman Museum's attendance fell below estimates while its operating costs ran far above them, and it laid off staff (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: Supports the case's own worry that "committing all remaining assets could limit her financial flexibility as the project develops" (case p.3)
critique: US arts centres and museums, far bigger than a residency
note: Groups that stayed flexible after building came through: field evidence for the case's warning against committing all remaining assets.

idea: Building campaigns often miss the endowment meant to run the building: one arts centre cost $400 million with $20 million raised for its endowment against an $80 million goal; another was $28 million in debt
sources: Grantmakers in the Arts blog on the study, https://www.giarts.org/blog/janet/set-stone; New York Times report of 28 Jun 2012 as reposted at https://abbesparksmedia.com/httpwww-nytimes-com20120628artsdesignstudy-shows-expansion-can-be-unhealthy-for-arts-groups-htmlpagewanted1refarts/ (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: Running money is what donors fund last, so Laura's prepaid running money is the scarce part of the residency's budget

idea: After Chicago's museum building boom, the Spertus Institute had laid off more than half its staff by 2012 and in January 2013 narrowed its mission and cut programmes for children and teens

idea: Raising the reserve after the building opens rarely works: "Continuing capital campaigns with the intention of raising reserve money or start-up funds after the building opens is often an exercise in futility"; campaign goals miss "the 'buckets of money' beyond project costs"

note: Same GIA article and 'exercise in futility' quote as Q11b-025, which is fuller (this row names the author, Katie Oman).

idea: Reserves come before buildings: "Building working capital and creating operating reserves should be an organization's first capitalization priority"; groups that cannot raise money "over and above operating costs" "should not take on building ownership"
sources: Nonprofit Finance Fund and Helicon Collaborative, "Critical Steps Toward Capital Health in the Cultural Sector" (2014), https://www.giarts.org/sites/default/files/critical-steps-toward-capital-health-cultural-sector.pdf (accessed 9 Nov 2026)

idea: Money not held apart gets spent on deficits: "Capital is episodic; revenue is forever"; capital is "typically not segregated from regular operating revenue"; and "capital, regardless of the purpose for which it is intended, will be used to cover structural operating deficits"
sources: Nonprofit Finance Fund, "Case for Change Capital in the Arts" (2011), https://www.giarts.org/sites/default/files/Case-for-Change-Captial-In-the-Arts.pdf; Brown and Nacht, "Lessons Learned about Change Capital in the Arts" (2014, evaluation of NFF's $15m Leading for the Future initiative), https://www.giarts.org/sites/default/files/lessons-learned-about-change-capital-arts-reflections-four-year-evaluation.pdf (accessed 9 Nov 2026)

idea: Deficits often arrive after the opening: NFF warns of being "house rich and cash poor", with surpluses during a campaign followed by deficits after completion; Kresge-backed campaigns added reserves to their goals

idea: In ordinary years a third or more of US arts groups run a deficit: 34% (2018), 35%, 33%, 24% (2021), 37%, 41%, 41% (2024), 34% (2025, preliminary); average working capital went from 8.6 months (2018) to a 16.4 peak (2021) and back to 9.9 (2025)
sources: SMU DataArts, National Trends 2026 data tables, https://culturaldata.org/national-trends/national-trends-2026/data-tables; National Trends 2025, https://www.culturaldata.org/national-trends/national-trends-2025: 44% ran a deficit in 2024; median working capital fell from 6.75 months (2021) to 4.25 months (2024) (accessed 9 Nov 2026)

idea: The typical arts group holds very little: in 2019 the average was 5 months of working capital but the median only 1.5 months; dance groups about two weeks, art museums about 11 months

note: The typical arts group holds about 1.5 months of working capital while Laura's commitment is bought a decade ahead (say it is her $50,000, not the whole budget).

idea: Thin reserves and thin margins predict closure: the Tuckman-Chang measures "show substantial promise for predicting the closure" of some arts nonprofits, were the best predictor of distress for performing arts groups, and predicted survival through the Great Recession
sources: Hager (2001), Nonprofit and Voluntary Sector Quarterly, "Financial Vulnerability among Arts Organizations: A Test of the Tuckman-Chang Measures", https://consensus.app/papers/details/7a00f4aa74965de9a88f7d58762de7a8/; Tevel and others (2014), Voluntas, https://consensus.app/papers/details/5cccadc22da35a09a32a0a75dcd179fe/ (implications for "surplus accumulation"); Graves and others (2023), https://consensus.app/papers/details/d203912fe25a5ffc9a059a28637b2e55/ (accessed 9 Nov 2026)

idea: Depending on grants is the danger, more than having few sources: "Greater vulnerability is associated with dependence on grant funding, not overall concentration"

idea: One-founder cultural institutions are fragile: private art museums that closed had been open a median of 10 years; closure was "usually related to financial difficulties, rather than the founder's death"; staying open "usually requires either ongoing financial contributions of their founders, or the establishment of a large endowment"

use: The closest reference class for a founder-led residency: Laura's ten prepaid years cover the window in which these closed, without depending on her later income

verified: VERIFIED (full-text PDF excerpts; report and site)

note: Top-40: founder-led private museums that closed lasted a median ten years and closed for money, the decade Laura's prepaid payments cover; say 2043 on is outside the plan.

idea: Yaddo (founded 1900) pays about 57% of its running costs from its endowment, which is about 65% shares; its cash covers under 3 months
sources: The Corporation of Yaddo, audited financial statements 2025, https://yaddo.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/The-Corporation-of-Yaddo-2025-FS-Final.pdf (accessed 9 Nov 2026): expenses $4,695,285; endowment appropriated for spending $2,289,342 plus a board-designated draw of $377,610; investments $39,324,300 (equity securities $25.4M); cash $1,052,062; spending rule 5% of a 12-quarter average; its "ability to meet its cash needs is dependent on continued contributions and investment market performance"
use: The residencies that last are carried by large endowments that rise and fall with markets; Laura's operating money is the opposite, fixed and dated
critique: Keel arithmetic: ($2,289,342 + $377,610) / $4,695,285 = 57% (2024: 55%); $25.4M / $39.3M = 65%; cash about 2.7 months of 2025 expenses. Yaddo is meant to last forever; Laura's commitment is ten years
note: Yaddo's running budget leans on a share-heavy endowment, the opposite of Laura's fixed, dated money.

idea: Yaddo nearly ended before its first guest: after Spencer Trask died in 1909 "the Trasks' financial investments depreciated the following year, jeopardizing Yaddo's future"; Katrina Trask closed the mansion in 1916 "to conserve what was left of the endowment"; the first guests came in 1926, 26 years after the founding corporation

critique: 1910s; the finding aid does not say what the Trasks' investments were
note: Top-40: Yaddo nearly closed before its first guest when its founders' investments fell, the risk the plan keeps away from the payments.

idea: MacDowell (1907) lasted because its founder kept raising running money: Marian MacDowell funded it "through a series of piano recitals and personal appeals" and gave lecture-recitals until her death in 1956; its director made "frequent trips to New York City to fund increasing operating expenses"; an endowment drive began in 1937; it has closed only twice (after the 1938 hurricane and in 2020)
sources: Library of Congress, MacDowell Colony records finding aid, https://findingaids.loc.gov/repositories/19/resources/2205 and http://hdl.loc.gov/loc.mss/eadmss.ms996002; https://www.macdowell.org/about; annual reports 2019 and 2020, https://www.macdowell.org/assets/media-center/newsletters/documents/2019_AnnualReport_FINAL2comp.pdf and https://www.macdowell.org/assets/media-center/newsletters/documents/2020_AnnualReport_FINAL.pdf (accessed 9 Nov 2026)

critique: Marian MacDowell had no fixed sum set aside; a founder's age and health matter in both stories
note: MacDowell's founder raised running money every year; the ladder does that once, in 2027, for ten years.

idea: Even a large residency endowment can fall 15% in a year: MacDowell's went from $33.1M to $28.2M in 2022 (investment return -$5.6M, after +$7.0M in 2021), while it ran a $3.4M gap before investment return
sources: MacDowell audited financial statements 2022, https://www.macdowell.org/assets/about/financial-information/MacDowell-Audited-Financial-Statements-2022-2-1.pdf (accessed 9 Nov 2026): expenses $5,812,785; change in net assets before investment return -$3,358,401; spending 5% of a 36-month average; a $5M line of credit, undrawn; a mortgage covenant requiring $7M of unrestricted liquid assets; a board-designated building and equipment reserve of $1,924,403; cash $750,115

idea: For the residencies that last, "a reserve" means a perpetual endowment, mostly in shares, plus people who keep raising money; Laura's operating reserve is something else: ten dated payments already bought
