idea: Taipei Artist Village, Taiwan's first public residency (12 Oct 2001), was set up by the Taipei Department of Cultural Affairs in a converted former public-works office, run by the Taipei Culture Foundation from 2004 (which added Treasure Hill on 2 Oct 2010), hosted more than 500 artists from over 40 countries, and lost its site: designated for public urban renewal, it moved out by the end of November 2023, ahead of a planned October 2024 move, and its programme went to Treasure Hill
sources: Taipei Artist Village, https://www.artistvillage.org/about.php; Taipei Culture Foundation 2023 final accounts, https://www.tcf.taipei/taipeicultureSysUpDoc/financial/5%E6%9C%AC-%E5%B8%83%E9%8A%85-%E6%96%87%E5%9F%BA%E6%9C%83_112%E5%B9%B4%E6%B1%BA%E7%AE%97%E6%9B%B8_%E5%AF%A9%E8%AD%B0%E9%80%9A%E9%81%8E.pdf (room occupancy 38.06% in 2023 as it wound down) (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: In Taiwan a residency can lose its building through no fault of its own; the IPS's three named risks do not include a lost site, but flexibility money is what would pay for a move
critique: A public site on public land; store H9-121 holds the founding (secondary)
note: A Taiwan residency lost its public site to urban renewal, a risk the IPS does not name that flexible money would pay for.

idea: Taipei's two public residencies run mostly on city money: the 2018 budget gave Taipei Artist Village NT$16.05m (city NT$11.17m, other government NT$0.20m, own income NT$4.67m, mostly rent; 5 staff) and Treasure Hill NT$37.05m (city NT$29.81m including NT$5.8m capital, other government NT$2.0m, own income NT$5.23m; 16 staff; staff costs NT$10.86m, security NT$3.43m, cleaning NT$2.40m)
sources: Taipei Culture Foundation, 2018 budget, https://www.tcf.taipei/taipeicultureSysUpDoc/financial/107%E5%B9%B4%E9%A0%90%E7%AE%97%E6%9B%B8_20230814175317.pdf (foundation-wide, government subsidy 67.28% of revenue); 2024 final accounts, https://www.tcf.taipei/taipeicultureSysUpDoc/financial/%E6%96%87%E5%9F%BA%E6%9C%83_113%E5%B9%B4%E6%B1%BA%E7%AE%97%E6%9B%B8_1140722_%E5%B8%82%E6%94%BF%E6%9C%83%E8%AD%B0%E7%89%88.pdf (Treasure Hill occupancy 73.38% in 2024, 72.95% in 2023) (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: Government share about 71% (Taipei Artist Village) and 86% (Treasure Hill); keeping a site guarded and clean was about 16% of Treasure Hill's budget: the building's running cost, not its construction (Keel arithmetic)
critique: Budgets, not actuals; 2018 prices; city-run, so not a model for a private residency
note: Taipei's public residencies run on 71% and 86% city money, budgets that are yearly and can be cut.

idea: Taiwan's national arts grant-maker never got its endowment: the law set a NT$10bn fund to be reached within 10 years; government gave its NT$6bn share by 2003, but the NT$4bn private share was never raised, and the fund is budgeted at NT$6.88bn at the end of 2025, under 70% of the target
sources: National Culture and Arts Foundation Act, https://law.moj.gov.tw/eng/LawClass/LawAll.aspx?pcode=H0000056; Legislative Yuan Budget Center, NCAF 2025 budget evaluation (11 Nov 2024), https://www.ly.gov.tw/Pages/ashx/File.ashx?FilePath=~%2FFile%2FAttach%2F246007%2FFile_19842001.pdf (「基金餘額仍未達法定數額」: the fund has still not reached its legal amount); LY evaluation page https://www.ly.gov.tw/Pages/Detail.aspx?nodeid=55923&pid=247583 (the 60% government, 40% private split; NT$2bn starting fund in 1996) (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: Private money promised to Taiwan's arts did not arrive even for the national fund: a pledge is not money in hand
critique: A government foundation, not a residency
note: Top-40: the private half of Taiwan's national arts fund was promised in law and never arrived, plain proof that a pledge is not money in hand.

idea: A grant-maker living on investment income gives less in bad years: NCAF's revenue fell from NT$318.8m (2014) to NT$188.9m (2015) when its return was 2.42% against 3.59% expected (financial income 79.7% of 2015 revenue; fund about NT$2bn each in deposits, shares and fixed income); its 2027 budget pays NT$7.302m of regular grants from a special reserve kept "to keep regular grants steady" and holds a NT$300m "Act for the Future" reserve set aside in 2021
sources: NCAF 2015 annual report (English), https://www.ncafroc.org.tw/files/publishBookEn/20200623/4fa69c5d236e4b53843284ca1e8553fc/4fa69c5d236e4b53843284ca1e8553fc.pdf; NCAF 2027 budget, https://www.ncafroc.org.tw/files/informationBudget/20260903/b324c6ad9912453d98bffdaa6591b2d8/b324c6ad9912453d98bffdaa6591b2d8.pdf (『「穩定常態補助款」特別公積』) (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: A Taiwan grant-maker or co-sponsor funded by returns can give less in the same years shares fall; Laura's payments do not depend on returns
critique: Keel arithmetic: NT$188.86m / NT$318.80m - 1 = -41%; the 2014 figure may include one-off items (not checked)
note: Same NCAF income fall as Q4b-026, which settles its cause; the grant-steadying reserve fits Q4b-027.

idea: Laura's $50,000 a year is about NT$1.64m: roughly a tenth of Taipei Artist Village's 2018 budget and 4.4% of Treasure Hill's

use: Context for co-sponsors: a strong base for a small residency, not a whole budget (agrees with store H9-119 for US residencies)
